title: The family of Benedict
hookLine: Cluny, the Cistercians, the Trappists: many branches of one Rule

lines: A TALL CHURCH AND LONG CHANT.
cards: Two monasteries. In the first, the church is tall and richly decorated, and the monks spend long hours in sung prayer, the liturgy unfolding in full ceremony.
In the second, the walls are plain, the windows clear, the monks out in the fields in rough habits, and the church so bare it almost echoes.
Ask the monks in either place what they live by, and they'll hand you the same small book. Today: the family of Benedict.

teach.b: Benedict wrote for monasteries, not for an order. Each house was its own family, under its own abbot. So how did one rule produce such different houses?
Part of the answer is in the Rule itself: it's built to bend.
In chapter eighteen, after laying out which psalms are sung when, Benedict says anyone who finds a better arrangement may use it, as long as the whole psalter is still prayed each week.

In chapter fifty-five, clothing should suit the place and the climate. Again and again the abbot is told to weigh things, adjusting for the weak and the strong. A rule that expects to be adapted gets adapted.
Cluny, in Burgundy in France, became known for its liturgy: long, splendid prayer in the choir, and other houses linked themselves to it.

The Cistercians took their name from Cîteaux, another French monastery, where monks set out to keep the Rule more strictly and simply: plain churches, hand labor, Benedict's life stripped back to its lines.
Saint Bernard of Clairvaux was a Cistercian.
And the Trappists, named for the abbey of La Trappe, came out of a reform within the Cistercians seeking a stricter observance still; officially they're the Cistercians of the Strict Observance.
Cluniacs and Cistercians argued, sometimes sharply, about what keeping the Rule really required. Yet each was reading the same chapters: listen, stay, bear with each other.

how: Benedictine, Cistercian and Trappist monasteries each follow the Rule of Saint Benedict, with their own constitutions and customs, and some welcome visitors to their prayer and retreat houses.

games.q: what does “the family of benedict” mean?
o: the houses and orders that all live by Benedict's Rule
Benedict's own relatives, including his sister
the first monks who lived with Benedict at one abbey

s: Benedict founded a centralized order with houses everywhere
he wrote for monasteries; each house was its own family under its own abbot.
the Rule itself allows some things to be arranged differently
chapter eighteen allows a better arrangement of the psalms, and chapter fifty-five fits clothing to the climate.
the Trappists follow a different rule from the Cistercians
they came out of a reform within the Cistercians and still live by Benedict's Rule.

games.q: you're a monk who thinks your house has drifted from the plain life Benedict describes. what do the Cistercians do?
o: throw out the Rule and write a new one.
set out to keep the same Rule more strictly and simply.
games.why: the Cistercians kept Benedict's Rule but stripped the life back: plain churches and hand labor. the Trappists later did the same within the Cistercians.

practice: Somewhere right now, in a house of one of these branches, monks and nuns are at work, or in choir, or asleep before an early office: the old one in the infirmary, the novice still learning the chants, the one in the kitchen.
If you pray, hold them before God for these two minutes; if you don't, simply keep them company in your attention, without needing to know their names.

wordCard.voice: The family of Benedict. The monasteries and orders that live by his Rule, Cluny, the Cistercians, the Trappists and others, each reading it in its own way. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: one rule, many houses. The branches argued, and still read the same book. That's today, done.
